title: Look Back to Move Forward: Learning to Revisit for Agentic Compositional Image Generation

paper.title: Look Back to Move Forward: Learning to Revisit for Agentic Compositional Image Generation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Text-to-image models have made remarkable progress in visual fidelity and instruction following, yet complex compositional generation remains challenging. Existing agentic approaches address this limitation through iterative generation and editing, adapting their actions based on interaction history.
However, they typically fix the continuation state ( i.e. , the image from which refinement proceeds) to the latest image.
Since iterative editing is not necessarily monotonic, the agent may continue refining from the latest image even when it has already degraded.
In this work, we introduce GenRevisit , an agentic framework that extends action selection to joint continuation-state and action selection .
The agent can not only use interaction history to adjust editing instructions but also select an image candidate to edit, jointly deciding where to continue from and how to refine .
We train GenRevisit with SFT followed by agentic reinforcement learning. To address the coarse credit assignment of final outcome reward in GRPO, which assigns the same trajectory-level advantage to all actions, we further propose Normalized Action Credit Assignment (NACA) to redistribute positive advantage according to each action’s contribution to reducing the remaining objective. On GenEval2, GenRevisit achieves GM scores of 84.3 and 74.4 with Qwen-Image-2512 and Z-Image-Turbo, surpassing the strongest baselines using the same generators by 12.7 and 10.9 points respectively. GenRevisit achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval, GenEval++, and GenEval2 among baselines.

GenRevisit achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval, GenEval++, and GenEval2 among baselines. 1 Introduction Recent text-to-image (T2I) models have made substantial progress in visual fidelity and instruction following [ 29 , 30 , 34 ] , while satisfying object counts, attributes, and spatial relations in a single generation attempt remains challenging [ 6 , 16 ] . To address this challenge, Iterative generation uses feedback on intermediate results to guide subsequent generation and editing [ 32 , 12 , 21 ] . As iterative generation produces multiple intermediate outcomes, the appropriate corrective action may vary from round to round. Fixed refinement procedures may therefore struggle to adapt to the evolving generation process, motivating an agentic sequential decision-making formulation in which the agent learns to select the next operation based on the accumulated interaction history [ 23 ] . Figure 1: An illustrative comparison between latest-state refinement and our GenRevisit. However, these policies mainly focus on learning what action to take next. An editing operation requires both a source image ( i.e. , the image from which refinement proceeds) and an editing instruction, but the source is often predetermined by the workflow. Although the interaction history records what action has attempted on each state and the resulting feedback, it works only for revising the instruction based on the fixed state if we just learn the action selection policy. This design has room for improvement because if we can’t jointly decide continuation state and action to do, we may miss more promising state to continue for better results. For example, as illustrated in Figure 1 , an edit to I 0 I_{0} produces I 1 I_{1} but violates previously satisfied constraints. A latest-only policy then gains additional feedback, yet its next edit must still start from the degraded image I 1 I_{1} . The agent may thus spend its limited budget restoring constraints that remain satisfied in I 0 I_{0} . This highlights the need for a policy that learns to jointly select a continuation state and specify an editing instruction tailored to it, rather than only adapting the instruction to a fixed source. To this end, we introduce GenRevisit, a framework that expands decision space from action selection to joint continuation-state and action selection. We treat image candidates accumulated in the interaction history as candidate continuation states, each corresponding to a possible starting point for further refinement. At each decision step, GenRevisit uses a multimodal planner to choose the next action from generation, editing, querying, and submission, based on decision context. When it edits, it jointly decides a source image and an editing instruction to correct remaining errors while preserving satisfied constraints. This allows the planner to revisit a stronger image candidate and open new refinement branches, rather than being restricted to the latest image. We train our proposed GenRevisit in two stages. First, we collect multi-round trajectories with GPT-5.5 and initialize the planner by supervised fine-tuning (SFT). We supervise actions that improve the image, including recovery from degraded states. Failed actions are excluded from the SFT loss but kept in the history with their feedback, because they still inform later decisions. We then use reinforcement learning (RL) with GRPO [ 31 ] to further improve the planner through its own interactions. The terminal reward measures how well the final submitted image satisfies the task constraints. However, the standard GRPO assigns the same advantage to every action in a trajectory, so a positive trajectory advantage can reinforce actions that worsen the image. To address this issue, we propose Normalized Action Credit Assignment (NACA). In positive-advantage trajectories, NACA redistributes credit among generation and editing actions based on the fraction of the remaining utility gap that each action closes. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of GenRevisit from three perspectives: (i) Compositional generation: GenRevisit achieves 84.3 GM on GenEval2 [ 16 ] , exceeding the strongest agentic baseline by 12.7 points. Results on GenEval [ 6 ] and GenEval++ [ 38 ] further support cross-benchmark generalization. (ii) Cross-generator transfer: We use GenRevisit with Z-Image-Turbo [ 39 ] without additional training. It also outperforms the strongest agentic baseline with the same generator by 10.9 points on GenEval2. (iii) Benefit of joint selection: Joint selection outperforms latest-only and best-only rules by 5.0 and 2.8 GM points, in matched-budget teacher continuations. The policy trained on joint demonstrations achieves 81.5 GM on GenEval2, exceeding its best-only-trained counterpart by 4.0 points. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose GenRevisit, a history-conditioned framework for joint continuation-state and action selection, making the choice of where to continue an explicit policy decision rather than a predetermined starting condition. • We combine action-level SFT with RL and introduce NACA, which redistributes image-action credit in positive-advantage trajectories according to normalized local progress. • GenRevisit achieves state-of-the-art performance on GenEval, GenEval++ and GenEval2 among baselines, surpassing the best GenEval2 results for Qwen-Image-2512 and Z-Image-Turbo by 12.7 and 10.9 points respectively, showing strong compositional generation. 2 Related Work Compositional evaluation. As text-to-image models are increasingly expected to satisfy constraints involving multiple objects, attributes, and relations simultaneously, compositional faithfulness has become a core test of generation capability. Earlier benchmarks such as GenEval, T2I-CompBench, and ConceptMix organize evaluation around predefined compositional dimensions [ 6 , 11 , 35 ] , whereas TIFA, Davidsonian Scene Graph, and GenEval 2 move toward prompt-specific atomic verification by decomposing each request into individually verifiable rubrics [ 10 , 4 , 16 ] . Inspired by this paradigm, we use constraint-level atomic judgments as fine-grained environment feedback for multi-round agentic generation, allowing decisions to be grounded in how individual constraints evolve across attempts. Iterative image generation. Iterative generation has progressed from prompt rewriting, repeated editing, and visual reflection [ 32 , 12 , 21 ] to closed-loop systems that evaluate intermediate results and invoke generation or editing tools accordingly [ 36 , 9 , 13 ] . More recent approaches make this feedback loop increasingly explicit: Qwen-Image-Agent incorporates verification feedback into subsequent refinement, while R3 organizes feedback-driven retry and repair [ 40 , 33 ] . Generation Navigator further formulates iterative generation as state-dependent action selection, learning when to stop, refine, or regenerate [ 23 ] . We build on this progression by extending the decision from what to do next to which source state to act from: historical candidates are retained as selectable branching points, allowing the policy to jointly choose a source state and the subsequent operation. 3 Preliminaries Agentic image generation can be viewed as a sequential decision process in which a planning policy interacts with external tools. Given a prompt specifying multiple compositional requirements, the objective is to produce an image that satisfies these requirements within a total budget of image generation and editing calls. At each decision step, the planner selects an action according to its planning policy, conditioned on the current decision context. The environment executes the action and updates the decision context with the resulting observations and feedback. We formalize this interaction in terms of states, actions, and trajectories. States and actions. Let x x denote the input prompt and B B the total budget of image generation and editing calls. At decision step t t , the interaction state s t s_{t} denotes the decision context available to the planning policy, including x x , the available history of actions, images, and feedback, and the remaining budget. The policy π θ \pi_{\theta} , parameterized by θ \theta , selects an executable action as a t ∼ π θ ( ⋅ ∣ s t ) . a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}). Each action specifies an operation and its associated parameters. Here, s t s_{t} represents the overall decision context rather than an individual image candidate. Interaction trajectories. The environment executes a t a_{t} and incorporates the resulting observations and feedback into the next decision state s t + 1 s_{t+1} . The sequence of interactions forms a trajectory τ = ( s 0 , a 0 , s 1 , a 1 , … , s T − 1 , a T − 1 , s T ) , \tau=(s_{0},a_{0},s_{1},a_{1},\ldots,s_{T-1},a_{T-1},s_{T}), where T T is the number of decision steps. The interaction terminates when a final image is selected as the output or another prescribed termination condition is met. The total number of generation and editing calls is bounded by B B and need not equal T T . While s t s_{t} denotes the complete interaction state available for decision making, image candidates accumulated in the interaction history serve as candidate continuation states, each representing a possible starting point for further refinement. We refer to the candidate selected for this purpose as the continuation state . Whether the continuation state is fixed to the latest candidate or explicitly selected from the interaction history is determined by the action interface. Section 4.1 describes a history-conditioned interaction framework that enables joint continuation-state and action selection. 4 Method An overview of our GenRevisit is shown in Figure 2 .
